title: Lego Mars Rover
description: Our group designed, built, and programmed a Lego Mars Rover to semi-autonomously traverse a "Martian landscape" to complete multiple tasks, including activating an Arduino communications array, within a five-minute limit, using color, touch, gyroscope, and range sensors to ensure accuracy and reliability.

timeline.heading: Objective
timeline.description: For our semester project, our objective was to create a LEGO Mars Rover designed to navigate a simulated Martian landscape and complete tasks like fueling a reactor, collecting samples, and activating a communications array, applying all the skills we learned throughout the semester to create a rover that could reliably complete these challenges within a 10-minute time limit. The rover begins centered on a black square, with it being randomly placed on 1 of the 4 different colored diagonals. The color won't be known prior to the start. From there, we will only be able to see a video stream of the robot every other minute during the mission starting from the 2nd minute for 1 minute at a time. During that minute, we can upload code to the robot. Activating the communcations array will allow us to see the robot for 80 seconds with a 40 second gap. Also, completing the fuel reactor task first will earn us extra credit.

timeline.heading: Brainstorming
timeline.description:
For this project, our robot had to complete a series of tasks in any order we'd like. So, we first had to figure out the order of the tasks. We decided to have the robot complete the tasks on the other side of the bridge before coming back and doing the rest since we got extra credit for doing so. We came up with this order based on how easy it was to transition between tasks:

1) Drop ball into Fuel Reactor
2) Push sample #1 (the bottle)
3) Drill wall
4) Activate Communications Array (Arduino)
5) Collect Soil Sample
6) Enter River Bed (enter & exit on different ramps)
7) Push sample #2.

I was tasked with coding 1 & 2, while Gavin coded 3 - 5, and Pranav coded 6 - 7.

timeline.heading: Initial Build
timeline.description: Our robot used tracks with rubber grips to ensure the robot doesn’t slip when going up the ramps. We also thought the tracks would ensure the robot moves straight, but this wasn't the case during testing, so we had to use the gyroscope to ensure the robot goes straight. Next, we included a ball holder driven by a large motor to hold and drop the ball in the fuel reactor, after which, the holder would be in a vertical position, acting as a wall to push the fuel samples with.

timeline.heading: Task 1: Orienting the Robot
timeline.description:
In the start, the robot is placed in the black square with the sensor over a random color we don't know. Regardless of color, the robot has to rotate and face the bridge.

I first decided to have the robot turn clockwise until the robot detects the red tape. Then, the robot turns 45 degrees clockwise using the gyroscope to line up with the bridge. During testing, the robot wasn’t consistently lining up with the bridge since the robot shifted while turning, causing inconsistencies with alignment. To account for that, I made the robot turn a set amount of degrees based on the color it's over, which fixed the issue.

timeline.heading: Task 2: Fuel Reactor
timeline.description:
After crossing the bridge, the robot has to drop the ball into the fuel reactor by lining up with the green tape and moving forward until it's next to the reactor.

Initially, I made the robot cross the bridge until it detected the green tape. It then turns right to align with the green tape and move forward until it detected the black tape. It drops the ball by lowering the arm and raising it again. However, during testing, the robot wasn’t aligning fully with the green tape, causing it to drift to the right. So, I changed the code to follow the edge of the green line, moving right if it's on the green line and left if it isn't.

timeline.heading: Task 3: Sample #1
timeline.description:
For this task, the robot has to move back from the fuel reactor until the red tape. Then, it needs to turn right, go straight a little, turn right again, and go straight to push sample #1 into the red box.

Gavin managed to get the robot to complete the task after tweaking the distances and turning angles.

timeline.heading: Task 4: Drill the Wall
timeline.description:
For this task, the robot needed to travel from sample 1 to the wall, where the robot would touch the wall to "drill" it.

This was a basic movement for the robot, as it needed to turn ~45 degrees and drive into the wall. To stop the robot, we used a button sensor. The code for this task was basic: set the yaw angle to 0, turn ~45 degrees, drive forward, and stop for 5 seconds when the button is pressed. Throughout the project, we had to make minor adjustments to the value of the yaw angle to make sure the robot was lined up for the next task.

resources.caption: Wall that needs to be drilled

timeline.heading: Task 5: Communications Array
timeline.description:
For this task, the robot has to get within 10cm of the communications array, which is an Arduino with a range sensor.  Afterwards, the Arduino needed to blink two colors for 10 seconds and then turn green when it detected the robot.

To drive the robot to the Arduino, we set it to back up from the wall until it sees red, turn 90 degrees, drive until it sees the black square, drive into the Arduino area, and stop to ensure the Arduino detects the robot. For the arduino, we used the range sensor to detect the robot, which then triggered the code to blink the colors. A variable was created to track if the array has been activated. Throughout the project, we needed to adjust where the robot backed into the Arduino’s zone so that the distance sensor could always detect the robot.

timeline.heading: Task 6: Soil Sample
timeline.description:
This task required us to stop on the yellow square for 5 seconds to collect soil samples. This was very basic for our robot because it required it to drive forward until it saw yellow simply.

At the beginning of our project, we had the robot simply drive forward after activating the Arduino and stopping on yellow; however, as we progressed, we decided to push sample #2 prior to drilling the yellow square for a more reliable program. To reach the yellow square, we decided to move the range sensor to the front, facing down to detect when the robot was close to the edge. This allowed us to detect the edge of the board, so after completing sample #2, we can simply move forward until the robot reaches the edge, and then turn left and move straight until it is in the yellow box.

timeline.heading: Task 7: River Bed Sample
timeline.description:
For this task, the rover had to go down one ramp onto the Dry River Bed, wait 5 seconds, and come back up on another ramp.  There were various lines of yellow tape on the ground that could be used to turn and orient the rover.  This part of the course was mostly for extra credit, but we decided to attempt to get all the points we could.

For this section, we tried a few different things with the code.  Going onto the other ramp relied heavily on the robot going straight, so we tried a different way of using the gyroscope to go straight to hopefully get the robot to go as straight as possible while also trying new methods of coding. The straight MyBlock when paired with a repeat until loop turned back to yaw 0 if off.  We also tried using the pitch to find when the robot angles down, then back up.

timeline.heading: Task 8: Sample #2
timeline.description: At first, we had the rover pushing sample 2 after it had gone around the dry river bed. This path was difficult as it was hard to get the robot to go straight across the whole board to hit the soil sample on target. It would often curve to the left or right and be slightly off to push the sample. To solve this problem, we moved this part of the code to after it activated the Arduino. After we edited the code, we found that it was much easier to get the second sample when the robot was closer. After the robot had activated the communications array, we added a section of code where it turned slightly, and moved forward until it hit black. From there, the robot simply moved forward, turned right, and moved the sample into place.

timeline.heading: Fail Safe Code
timeline.description: In the event our robot does something unexpected, we created a fail safe file that allows us to control the robot to move forward or turn so it can return back to its intended path. However, we could only view and change the code every 1 minute for a minute, so we couldn't use it whenever we wanted.

timeline.heading: Launches
timeline.description: On launch day, we tested our robot a few times before launch by running all our code at once, which the robot did successfully. However, when we did the launch, we decided to make the robot stop at certain checkpoints to allow us to make corrections if necessary. This caused the robot to fail since splitting the code up into different sections caused our yaw measurements to reset unexpectedly, causing the robot to move in the wrong direction. During our second attempt, we tried to prevent this by running the code all at once, as we did during testing, but the robot immediately fell off the ramp, which essentially ruined our attempt. This time, we learned that stopping the robot was necessary to prevent mistakes like this. We ran it once more, which ultimately resulting in a successful launch.

timeline.heading: Final Thoughts
timeline.description: Overall, this project was a great way to end the semester. Throughout this project, I had to use the various concepts we learned during the semester to complete the various tasks. The sensor project we had earlier in the semester was very useful as I relied heavily on the stuff I learned in that project to complete the tasks. However, getting the robot to complete the tasks was a huge challenge for our group. Not only was the robot behaving unexpectedly at certain times, but it was also very inconsistent and imprecise. To counter these issues, our group had to take advantage of the sensors and use the features of  the track to guide the robot through. While it did take some time, we managed to get the robot to complete all the tasks on sol 16.In the end, I think this could’ve been prevented by simulating the launch conditions before launching the robot and testing all our failsafes to make sure we knew what to do on the actual launch. Despite our failures, this project has been very fun and I learned a lot from it that I could use for other engineering projects in the future.
